subject: technology
essential_question: How can understanding networks, cybersecurity, and digital safety help us explain, decide, create, or solve something that matters?
standards: Michigan Computer Science: Networks and Internet
project_brief: Complete a fictional security audit and create a response plan without testing real systems. This is the grade 7 culminating project for "Networks, Cybersecurity, and Digital Safety" (ma-g7-technology-u05, unit 5), built around network basics, encryption concept, authentication, phishing and social engineering, and updates and backups. Diagram or organize the system described in this unit (covering network basics, encryption concept, authentication, and phishing and social engineering) and write a step-by-step protocol someone else could follow to reproduce your result or troubleshoot the same problem.
requirements: Address every topic listed for this unit: network basics, encryption concept, authentication, phishing and social engineering, updates and backups, and incident reporting.
Meet the performance task as written: Complete a fictional security audit and create a response plan without testing real systems.
Show your work or process, not just a final result — a process note, sketch log, commit history, or draft trail.
Complete the checklist in this package before submitting.
primary_task: Diagram or organize the system described in this unit (covering network basics, encryption concept, authentication, and phishing and social engineering) and write a step-by-step protocol someone else could follow to reproduce your result or troubleshoot the same problem.
test_or_check_criteria: Every claim or design choice in the submission can be traced to network basics or another named topic from this unit — nothing is left unexplained.
The submission runs, displays, or demonstrates correctly on at least two different sample inputs or scenarios the student chooses.
No real password, API key, account credential, precise location, or other real personal/system data appears anywhere in the submission — fictional or sandbox examples only.
The student can explain, in their own words, why each step or decision was made, not just that it works.

presentation_and_privacy.sandbox_and_credentials_note: This project never touches a real account, a real password or API key, a live production system, or another person's real data. Use fictional names, sandbox environments, local files, or already-approved sample data throughout. Submit code, screenshots of your own sandbox, diagrams, or a written walkthrough — a live public deployment is never required.

copyright_and_authorship: The final submitted work must remain your own authorship. A parent, tutor, or AI assistant may help you plan, explain a concept, demonstrate a technique, or give feedback on a draft, but may not produce the graded work itself. Never request, store, or submit a real password, API key, access token, or other real credential; use only fictional accounts and sandboxed or offline systems.
remediation: If the project stalls, step back to the smallest version of the task: rebuild just the part covering network basics in isolation, using a worked example from this unit as a model, then re-attach it to the full project once that smaller piece works and you can explain why.
extension: Once the core project is working, extend it to handle a new constraint or edge case related to encryption concept, or compare two different approaches to the same problem and explain the real tradeoff between them in your own words.
